content: The Guideline Development Group (GDG) evaluated the evidence and made judgments based on the relative effect sizes, which are detailed in the research evidence. Beneficial Outcomes: Reactive Indoor Residual Spraying (RIRS) significantly reduces the prevalence of malaria, with a reduction of 27 cases per 1,000 persons (95% confidence interval [CI]: -35 to -8 per 1,000 persons) based on one cluster-randomized controlled trial (cRCT) with a superiority design and high-certainty evidence. RIRS may reduce the incidence of clinical malaria; however, the effects are variable, and it is possible that RIRS has little to no impact. The reduction was estimated at 14 cases per 1,000 person-years (95% CI: -32 to 4 per 1,000 person-years) based on one cRCT with a superiority design and moderate-certainty evidence. Adverse Events: RIRS results in little to no difference in reported adverse events, with a risk difference (RD) of 2 events per 1,000 persons (95% CI: -2 to 1 per 1,000 persons) based on one cRCT with a superiority design and high-certainty evidence. RIRS also results in little to no difference in serious adverse events, including deaths, compared to standard IRS. This conclusion is based on one cRCT with a non-inferiority design and high-certainty evidence. Additional Findings: In a study involving 4,082 participants, no significant differences in serious adverse events were observed between RIRS and standard IRS. Another study with 2,000 participants reported similar findings, with no adverse events directly attributed to IRS. A larger study involving 393,387 participants found no significant differences in malaria-related deaths between the reactive IRS and standard IRS groups. Specifically, 9 deaths were reported in the reactive IRS arm out of a population of 204,237, compared to 12 deaths in the standard IRS arm out of a population of 189,150. Study Design and Limitations: The evidence includes data from randomized controlled trials, with some studies designed as non-inferiority trials comparing reactive IRS to standard IRS. While there was no serious inconsistency, indirectness, or publication bias in the evidence, some studies were affected by serious imprecision due to overlapping confidence intervals or limited sample sizes. Conclusion: Reactive IRS appears to be effective in reducing malaria prevalence and may have a modest impact on clinical malaria incidence. It does not significantly increase the risk of adverse events or deaths compared to standard IRS. These findings are supported by highto moderate-certainty evidence from multiple studies.
